html:
The making of a great world map and geography by the Arab scholar Muhammad al-Idrisi at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily in Palermo, finished in 1154.

Al-Idrisi was born in Ceuta, on the African side of the Strait of Gibraltar, around 1100, and studied in Córdoba in al-Andalus. He travelled widely. Around 1138 Roger, whose island kingdom had been taken from Muslim rulers by the Normans and still had many Muslim subjects, see the Emirate of Sicily, invited him to Palermo.

For some fifteen years al-Idrisi gathered the reports of travellers, merchants and sailors, checking them against each other. The result, known as the Book of Roger or Tabula Rogeriana, divides the known world into climate zones and sections, with maps and text, from the Atlantic to China. As was usual on Arab maps, south is at the top. A large world map was also engraved on a silver disc, now lost.

It was one of the most accurate maps of the medieval world, and a sign of how Arab, Greek and Latin learning met in Norman Sicily.
sum: The making of a great world map and geography by the Arab scholar Muhammad al-Idrisi at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily in Palermo, finished in 1154.
